faculty.name: Leila Bighash
faculty.title: Assistant Professor
faculty.bio: Leila Bighash is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Communication at the University of Arizona. Her research examines how people navigate information in organizations, particularly how information visibility influences what people can know and infer about one another and their environments. Her work focuses on communication networks, privacy, uncertainty, and expertise recognition across digital and organizational settings. Her work examines questions such as how people gain information by observing others’ interactions, how visible connections can signal expertise, and how the structure of an organization’s information environment can shape uncertainty and employee attitudes. She uses a range of methods, including experiments, surveys, social network analysis, and digital trace data. Her research has appeared in journals including Communication Theory , Management Communication Quarterly , Computers in Human Behavior , and the International Journal of Communication . Bighash earned her Ph.D. in Communication from the University of Southern California’s Annenberg School for Communication and Journalism. She teaches courses in organizational communication, communication technology, research methods, and communication networks. Dr. Bighash will not be accepting graduate students for Fall 2027. Selected Publications Gillig, T., Bighash, L. , & Shaikh, S. (2024).

faculty.name: Joseph Bonito
faculty.title: Professor
research_areas: Research methods related to the study of small groups
Machine learning applications to small group interaction
faculty.bio: Dr. Bonito earned his Ph.D. in 1997 at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign in the Department of Speech Communication. His primary area of interest is small group communication processes, especially characteristics of participation. He is always interested in small group research methods, including multilevel measurement models, and applying machine learning to the study of small group interaction. His articles have appeared in Communication Monographs , Human Communication Research , Communication Yearbook , Communication Research , Journal of Communication , Small Group Research , and Health Communication . He is the 2003 and 2013 recipient of the Dennis Gouran Award, given to the author of the outstanding monograph in small group communication by the Group Communication Division of the National Communication Association. He also received several top paper awards from the NCA Group Communication Division. Dr. Bonito was a co-investigator on a large grant from the National Cancer Institutue that evaluated communication and decision-making practices of the North American of Quitline Consortium (NAQC). He has also received several smaller grants through the University of Arizona. He teaches graduate and undergraduate courses in small group communication, communication and cognition, and research methods. Dr.

faculty.name: Jake Harwood
faculty.title: Professor; Director of Graduate Studies
faculty.bio: Jake Harwood (PhD, Univ. of California, Santa Barbara) is a Professor of Communication. His CV is here. His research focuses on intergroup communication with a particular focus on age groups and the role of music in intergroup relations. He is also interested in the use of AI LLMs for coding text data as well as agent-based modeling of communication processes. He authored "Communication and Music in Social Interaction" (Cognella, 2018) and “Understanding Communication and Aging” (3rd Edition, Cognella, 2023). He has published over 150 articles and book chapters, including recent publications in Media Psychology, Psychology of Music, and Nature Reviews Psychology . He is a Fellow of the International Communication Association. He teaches courses in research methods/statistics, intergroup communication, communication and music, and intergenerational communication. Dr. Harwood will not be accepting graduate students for Fall 2027. Projects Ongoing research projects with my graduate research team are examining intergroup contact and communication and the role of music in interpersonal and intergroup relations. We are also experimenting with using LLMs to code text data. Selected Publications ***Complete CV here. Selected Books: Giles, H., & Harwood, J. (Eds.) (2018). faculty.name: Kate Kenski
faculty.title: Professor
faculty.bio: Dr. Kate Kenski (Ph.D. 2006, University of Pennsylvania) is a Professor in the Department of Communication where she teaches political communication, public opinion, and research methods. Prior to teaching at the University of Arizona, she was a senior analyst at the Annenberg Public Policy Center at the University of Pennsylvania. She is co-author of The Obama Victory: How Media, Money, and Message Shaped the 2008 Election (2010, Oxford University Press) and Capturing Campaign Dynamics: The National Annenberg Election Survey (2004, Oxford University Press). She is co-editor of The Oxford Handbook of Political Communication with Kathleen Hall Jamieson. Dr. Kenski has published over 70 book chapters, articles, and research notes in publications such as the American Behavioral Scientist , the Annals of the American Academy of Political and Social Science , Communication Research , the International Journal of Public Opinion Research , the Journal of Applied Social Psychology , and Public Opinion Quarterly . Her current research focuses on social media and incivility, gender and politics, and online platform development that aids users’ quality of reasoning. Dr. Kenski will be accepting graduate students for Fall 2027. Selected Publications Kenski, K., Filer, C., & Conway-Silva, B. A. (2018).

faculty.name: Matthew A. Lapierre
faculty.title: Associate Professor
faculty.bio: Professor Lapierre (Ph.D., University of Pennsylvania) is an Associate Professor of Communication. His research explores how media affects health and well-being, particularly among children/families. Research projects include the influence of marketing cues on children’s consumer behavior, the development of children’s persuasion awareness/susceptibility, how parents contend with their children’s media use, how media engagement influences gun attitudes among adults and children, young people's responses to science communication, and the effects of various types of political communication (e.g., bad faith) on audience perceptions. If you would like an automatically updated list of publications or links to journal articles, you can check out Dr. Lapierre’s Google Scholar page here . Professor Lapierre is interested in working with graduate students who would like to conduct research on the topics identified above. Please email Dr. Lapierre directly ( mlapierre@arizona.edu ) if you would like more information about his work in these areas. Students who come from underrepresented populations in academia (e.g., students of color, and first-generation college students) are strongly encouraged to reach out. Dr. Lapierre will be accepting graduate students for Fall 2027.

faculty.name: Rain Wuyu Liu
faculty.title: Associate Professor
faculty.bio: Rain Wuyu Liu (Ph.D., Michigan State University, 2017) is an Associate Professor of Communication. Her research centers on persuasion and social influence, with a particular focus on the effects of social norm messaging on health and environmental information processing, attitude formation, and behavior change. She is also interested in the intersection of cultural values, beliefs, and social normative influence in shaping individuals’ attitudes and behaviors. Her work extends to research methods and strategic communication campaign design. With extensive experience in grant-funded research, Dr. Liu is a fellow at the Udall Center for Studies in Public Policy (the 37 th cohort) and has contributed to projects including a National Science Foundation (NSF) funded study among Tibetan herders on the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau. She has also worked on projects supported by the Michigan Department of Natural Resources (MDNR), the University of Arizona Research Innovation & Impact (RII), and the Social & Behavioral Sciences Research Institute (SBSRI). In addition, she is actively engaged in community-based initiatives and collaborates with environmental advocacy groups, such as S ustainable Tucson , to translate research into meaningful local impact.

faculty.name: Tae Joon Moon
faculty.title: Assistant Professor; Endowed Professorship in Alcohol Studies and Communication
faculty.bio: Dr. Tae Joon Moon is an Assistant Professor of Communication and Endowed Professor in Communication and Alcohol Studies. Prior to his role at the University of Arizona, he served as an Assistant Professor in the Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences, as well as in the School of Public Health at the University of Texas San Antonio. Dr. Moon’s research is dedicated to the design, development, and implementation of technology-enhanced interventions for individuals impacted by alcohol and/or substance use disorders. He leverages advanced healthcare technologies, such as remote biosensors and mobile health applications, to enhance the accessibility and the effectiveness of treatment for these conditions. His current research initiatives have expanded to encompass community-based interventions that aim to enhance awareness about the risks associated with excessive alcohol consumption and to improve accessibility to treatment for individuals facing alcohol-related challenges. He has been actively engaged in NIH-funded research projects, taking on roles as both Principal Investigator (PI) and Co-Investigator (Co-I). Dr. Moon has also contributed to the academic community through a series of peer-reviewed publications.
faculty.notes: Also holds the Endowed Professorship in Alcohol Studies and Communication.

faculty.name: Margaret J. Pitts
faculty.title: Associate Professor of Communication
faculty.bio: Maggie Pitts (PhD, Penn State, 2005) is Associate Professor in the Department of Communication at the University of Arizona. Maggie employs qualitative research methods to explore positive communication in contexts such as interpersonal communication, intercultural communication, and communication and aging. Positive communication refers to communication behaviors and practices that enhance personal and relational wellbeing and contribute to human flourishing (like communication savoring!). Maggie is one of the co-founders of the Positive Communication Network . Positive Communication Scholarship (1) is rigorous scientific inquiry into the nature of communication excellence, (2) focuses on both process and outcomes and is designed to generate new knowledge, (3) takes an affirmative stance, and (4) cultivates communication praxis. Toward this end, Maggie is finishing an edited book, the Handbook of Positive Communication and Aging to be published by Elgar Publishing. She serves on the editorial board for the Palgrave Studies in Positive Communication.

faculty.name: Steve Rains
faculty.title: Professor
faculty.bio: Steve Rains is a Professor of Communication. His research is situated in the areas of health communication, social influence, and communication and technology. He is interested in better understanding how and why messages influence people, particularly in health contexts and when using communication technologies. His work in recent years has primarily focused on social support, though he routinely studies digital coping, incivility, persuasion resistance, and related topics. He is especially interested in leveraging computational social science techniques to explore the dynamic communication processes involved in these phenomena. Dr. Rains currently serves as co-editor of the journal Communication Research. Dr. Rains will not be accepting graduate students for Fall 2027. Selected Publications A complete list of publications

faculty.name: Chris Segrin
faculty.title: Regents Professor; Steve and Nancy Lynn Professor of Communication
faculty.bio: Chris Segrin (Ph.D. 1990, University of Wisconsin) is a behavioral scientist whose specialty is interpersonal relationships and mental health. His research focuses on social skills, relationship development and satisfaction, and such problems as depression, anxiety, loneliness, and marital distress. This research can be found in journals such as Human Communication Research, Communication Monographs, Journal of Abnormal Psychology, Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology, Communication Research , and Journal of Psychosocial Oncology . He is author of the books Interpersonal Processes in Psychological Problems (2001), Family Communication (2026), and Conflict Communication (2026). Professor Segrin was also the editor of the journal Communication Theory from 2003-2005. In addition to his appointment in the Department of Communication, Professor Segrin is an Adjunct Professor of Psychology and Family Studies. Prior to joining the faculty at the University of Arizona, Professor Segrin was on the faculty of the University of Kansas and the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee. He teaches classes in interpersonal communication, nonverbal communication, persuasion, marriage and family, and research methods. Professor Segrin has been the recipient of six teaching awards from the University of Wisconsin, University of Kansas, and University of Arizona.
faculty.notes: Regents Professor; Steve and Nancy Lynn Professor of Communication.

faculty.name: Jennifer Stevens Aubrey
faculty.title: Department Head; Professor
faculty.bio: Dr. Jennifer Stevens Aubrey (Ph.D., University of Michigan, 2004) teaches classes on media, mass communication theory, and child and adolescent development in the Department of Communication at the University of Arizona. With an emphasis on gender and child/adolescent development, her research focuses on media effects on emotional, mental, and physical health in young people. Topically, her research tends to centers on issues related to sexuality and body image. Her research has been published in such top-tier journals as Health Communication , Media Psychology , and Journal of Communication . Dr. Stevens Aubrey will be accepting graduate students for Fall 2027. faculty.name: Rita Tang
faculty.title: Assistant Professor, Communication
faculty.bio: Dr. Rita Tang (Ph.D. 2026, University of Minnesota) is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Communication at the University of Arizona. She studies how people encounter, evaluate, and respond to contested information on social media, and how organizations can use AI and other tools to counter misinformation in health, science, and crisis communication. Her recent work examines how people understand, trust, and develop literacy about AI, and how correction experiences relate to their beliefs, democratic attitudes, and political participation. She uses mixed methods, including experiments, surveys, computational approaches, interviews, and thematic analysis. At Arizona, she teaches courses in health communication as well as social media and communication. Her research has appeared in journals including New Media & Society , Health Communication , Journal of Health Communication , Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly , Social Media + Society , and the Harvard Kennedy School Misinformation Review . She completed her Ph.D. in Mass Communication, with a minor in Political Psychology, at the Hubbard School of Journalism and Mass Communication, and holds an M.A. in Anthropology and Education from Teachers College, Columbia University, and a B.A. in Advertising from Fudan University. Dr. Tang will be accepting new graduate students for Fall of 2027.
